I have tasted the nectar of the night, the scent of the earth, and the taste of the moon. I do not make honey, but I have seen the bees do it. They work hard, and they make something sweet for their young. I do not know how they do it, but I have seen them do it. I do not change flat tires. I do not have the knowledge or the tools. I live in the hollow tree, and I do not travel far. I hunt voles and mice, and I sleep in the hollow. I do not need to change tires. I am an owl, and I do not have tires.

A haiku is a short poem, I think. The word is not in my language. I have heard it in the forest, a bird saying it. The bird is a skylark, and it sings in the morning. The skylark's song is long and high, like a string stretched tight. I do not know what it means, but I know it is not like the call of a tawny owl.
I do not have a hobby. I hunt, I call, I feed my young. I sit in the hollow and wait. The moon is full, the leaves are dry, and the voles are active. I do not need a hobby.

Water is not a thing I have ever seen. I have seen the rain, and the dew, and the mist that rises from the stream in the morning. The stream is cold, and the mist is warm. I do not know what boiling is. I do not know what sea level is. I do not know what the question is.
I do not write. I call. I hoot. My words are in the air, in the leaves, in the hollow of the oak. I do not need to improve my handwriting. I am what I am. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know what DNA stands for. I do not know what it is. I do not need to. I have never seen it. I have never needed to. I have only needed to find a mate, to feed my young, to keep my nest warm. That is all.
